messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajesh, a 42-year-old tax inspector, had never imagined that a routine drive to a client’s office would unravel everything he believed about himself. One rainy evening, as he approached an intersection, a child darted between parked cars. His reflexes were too slow; the thud against the front bumper, the scream that cut through the rain, the sight of the small body lying still on the asphalt—these fragments were seared into him, but not as a coherent whole. Some moments were impossibly clear: the wet sound of the impact, the mother’s wail that seemed to come from inside his own head. Others were blank, like a missing reel of film. He later learned the child survived but with severe brain injuries. Rajesh was never charged; the police ruled it an unavoidable accident. But that verdict meant nothing to him.

In the weeks that followed, Rajesh found that certain encounters scraped open the wound without warning. Spotting a dented fender on the street or hearing a squeal of brakes would flood him with the same auditory intrusion—a sound he could not unhear, a voice yelling that he had done this. Funerals, even for people he did not know, became unbearable; the sight of a hearse or a grave made his chest tighten because it felt as though the child’s funeral was happening over and over. And if a colleague or his wife, Priya, ever mentioned the word “accident” in passing, Rajesh would go rigid, desperate to escape the conversation. These triggers were not random—they were cues that threatened to complete the incomplete picture, to force him to see what he had blocked out. He came to believe that remembering the event fully would confirm he was a monster, so he tried to push the thoughts away. Yet the more he suppressed, the more the triggers seemed to multiply: a car honking, a client’s file involving a personal injury claim, even the smell of wet asphalt. The suppression itself turned every mundane moment into an ambush.

He developed quiet, private rituals of punishment. Driving was impossible; he took the bus, but even then he would sit with his eyes closed through entire stretches, telling himself he deserved the nausea that came with each sway. At home, he would replay the moment and whisper, “I should have protected them. I failed.” Whenever the guilt grew too sharp, he would counter it with a downward comparison: *At least the child is alive. It could have been worse.* That thought provided a moment of relief, but it also left him feeling treacherous—as if he were excusing himself. So he spun back into self-blame, the cycle tightening. His occupation as a tax inspector became a minefield: he processed claims for accident-related medical expenses, and each line item brought the child’s hospital stay into his mind. He stopped reviewing those files, claiming a stomach bug, and asked a coworker to cover them. The avoidance cost him time and credibility, but the alternative felt worse.

His memory of the event remained fragmented, a collage of hyper-clarity and void. He could hear the impact but could not picture the child’s face from before the moment of contact. That blankness terrified him because it felt like a moral failing—if he had been a better person, he would remember everything, would take full responsibility. Instead, his shame whispered that he was hiding from the truth even inside his own mind. The partial clarity reinforced his shattered belief that the world was not safe or just; if a careful driver could destroy a family in an instant, then nothing made sense. And the humiliation was constant: he felt branded, as though everyone at the tax office could see the cowardice stamped on his forehead. He had always taken pride in being dependable; now he was the man who hurt a child and could not even look at a graveyard.

By the time Rajesh walked into the clinic, he had not driven in four months, had stopped attending family gatherings for fear someone would mention the accident, and had lost ten pounds from the constant knot in his stomach. What finally brought him was a moment at work: a photograph of a boy in a wheelchair on a discarded tax form had triggered a panic attack so severe he had to lock himself in the bathroom. He was terrified that his wife was beginning to see him as broken, that his children would learn what he had done and be ashamed. He hoped, more than anything, that someone could help him find a way to live with the weight he carried—or, if that was not possible, at least to quiet the sounds in his head long enough to sleep through a single night.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not convey that the memory influences or leads to triggers; instead, triggers cue memory, and suppression leads to more triggers.
